concepts.title: Vanishing Point (Motion)
concepts.one_liner: The vanishing point is the location in the image plane where a point moving in a straight line with constant velocity converges as time goes to infinity.
concepts.content:
Consider a point moving in a straight line in 3D with constant velocity $\dot{\mathbf{P}} = (V_X, V_Y, V_Z)^\mathsf{T}$. At any time $t$, the point location is $\mathbf{P}(t) = (X+V_Xt, Y+V_Yt, Z+V_Zt)^\mathsf{T}$. Its 2D projection is given by:

$$\begin{aligned} x(t) &= f \frac{X + V_X t}{Z + V_Z t}\\ y(t) &= f \frac{Y + V_Y t}{Z + V_Z t} \end{aligned}$$

If the velocity component in $Z$ is non-zero ($\dot{Z} \neq 0$), the projected point converges to a vanishing point as $t \to \infty$:

$$\begin{aligned} \lim_{t \to \infty} x(t) &= f \frac{V_X}{V_Z} = x_{\infty}\\ \lim_{t \to \infty} y(t) &= f \frac{V_Y}{V_Z} = y_{\infty} \end{aligned}$$

(see figure: Projection onto the camera plane of the sequence produced by a bird flying away. The bird will vanish at the **vanishing point**)

The location of the vanishing point $\mathbf{p}_{\infty}=(x_{\infty}, y_{\infty})^\mathsf{T}$ is independent of the initial position of the point and depends only on the 3D velocity vector $\mathbf{V}$. Consequently, multiple points moving with the same velocity will converge to the same vanishing point.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding vanishing points in motion allows us to determine the direction of 3D travel from 2D image sequences, as all objects sharing a velocity vector will appear to head toward the same image coordinate.

concepts.title: Camera Translation Motion Field
concepts.one_liner: The camera translation motion field describes the 2D velocity of image points resulting from a camera moving in a straight line through a static scene.
concepts.content:
When a camera moves through a static scene with velocity $\dot{\mathbf{T}} = \mathbf{V} = (V_X,V_Y,V_Z)^\mathsf{T}$, every point $\mathbf{P}$ in the scene moves relative to the camera with velocity $\dot{\mathbf{P}} = -\mathbf{V}$. The resulting 2D motion field in the image plane is:

$$\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x} \\ \dot{y} \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{Z} \begin{bmatrix} -f & 0 & x \\ 0 & -f & y \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} V_X\\ V_Y \\ V_Z \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$

This relationship can be rearranged to make the contribution of the camera coordinates more explicit:

$$\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x} \\ \dot{y} \end{bmatrix} = -\frac{f}{Z} \begin{bmatrix} V_X\\ V_Y \end{bmatrix} + \frac{V_Z}{Z} \begin{bmatrix} x\\ y \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$

This provides a general expression for observed motion produced by camera translation without rotation.
concepts.motivation_md: By modeling how camera movement translates into image motion, we can separate the effects of the camera's own path from the movement of independent objects in a scene.

]

concepts.title: Lateral Camera Motion
concepts.one_liner: Lateral camera motion occurs when a camera translates parallel to the image plane, causing image points to move in the opposite direction at speeds inversely proportional to their depth.
concepts.content:
Lateral camera motion occurs when a camera translates parallel to the camera plane, meaning the forward velocity $V_Z = 0$. (see figure: Lateral camera motion parallel to the camera plane.)

In this case, the relationship between the 3D velocity and the apparent 2D velocity in the image plane is:

$$\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x} \\ \dot{y} \end{bmatrix} = -\frac{f}{Z} \begin{bmatrix} V_X \\ V_Y \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$

The motion field depends on the depth $Z$ at each location. Objects closer to the camera appear to move faster than objects farther away, while very distant objects appear stationary. This parallax effect is the same principle used in stereo vision to recover depth. The 2D motion in the image plane is always in the opposite direction to the camera's translation.

(see figure: Sketch of the motion field under lateral camera motion. Objects close to the camera will appear to be moving faster than objects farther away. Objects that are very far (like the cloud) will appear...)
concepts.motivation_md: Lateral motion is a common scenario (e.g., looking out a car window) where depth can be inferred from the relative speeds of objects, a phenomenon known as motion parallax.

concepts.title: Camera Forward Motion
concepts.one_liner: Camera forward motion occurs when a camera moves along its optical axis, resulting in a radial expansion of the image from a central point.
concepts.content:
For a camera moving forward along its optical axis, the lateral velocity components are zero ($V_X = V_Y = 0$) and the motion is only along the $Z$-axis ($V_Z \neq 0$). (see figure: Camera moving forward, along the camera axis.)

The resulting motion field is defined by:

$$\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x} \\ \dot{y} \end{bmatrix} = \frac{V_Z}{Z} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Forward motion is critical for navigation and obstacle avoidance, as it creates a characteristic expansion pattern that reveals the direction of travel and the proximity of objects.

]

concepts.title: Time to Contact
concepts.one_liner: Time to contact is the ratio of an object's depth to the camera's forward velocity, representing how long until the camera reaches that object.
concepts.content: The observed motion in a forward-moving camera depends on the ratio $V_Z/Z$, which is the inverse of the time to contact. The time to contact is the duration it will take the camera to reach an object located at distance $Z$ when moving at velocity $V_Z$. Notably, the rate of expansion in the image does not depend on the focal length $f$.
concepts.motivation_md: Time to contact is a vital cue for biological and robotic systems to avoid collisions, as it can be estimated directly from the expansion of the image without knowing the absolute distance or speed.

concepts.title: Focus of Expansion
concepts.one_liner: The focus of expansion is the point in the image plane where the observed motion is zero during forward camera translation.
concepts.content:
The observed motion is zero at the focus of expansion, located at $(x_{\infty}, y_{\infty})$. (see figure: Sketch of the motion field when the camera approaches a planar surface. The motion field indicates the rate of expansion of the image, and it is a function of the time to contact. In this example...)

When a camera approaches a surface, points near the center (the point of impact) appear stationary, while points in the periphery appear to move faster and away from the center. This creates an effect where the whole image expands over time from the focus of expansion.
concepts.motivation_md: The focus of expansion identifies the exact direction the camera is heading, making it a fundamental reference point for visual navigation and steering.

concepts.title: Euler Angles (Yaw, Pitch, Roll)
concepts.one_liner: Euler angles decompose a camera's rotation into yaw, pitch, and roll along the three coordinate axes.
concepts.content: To derive the rotation, we consider the Euler angles and decompose the rotation using rotations along the three axes (yaw, pitch, roll): (see figure: Rotation expressed by Euler angles (yaw, pitch, roll).) Each angle measures the rotation along the camera-coordinate axes. Using this representation of the rotation, the rotation matrix can be written as: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{R}_{\Delta t} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos \theta_Z & \sin \theta_Z & 0\\ -\sin \theta_Z & \cos \theta_Z & 0\\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \cos \theta_Y & 0 & -\sin \theta_Y\\ 0 & 1 & 0\\ \sin \theta_Y & 0 & \cos \theta_Y \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & \cos \theta_X & \sin \theta_X \\ 0 & -\sin \theta_X & \cos \theta_X \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$ In this equation, the sign of the angles are chosen to reflect that a rotation of the camera is equivalent to the opposite rotation of the 3D point.
concepts.motivation_md: Euler angles provide an intuitive way to represent complex 3D rotations as a sequence of three independent rotations around the principal axes, which is essential for modeling camera movement in computer vision.
concepts.recap_md: - Euler angles decompose a 3D rotation into yaw, pitch, and roll components.

Each angle measures the rotation along the camera-coordinate axes. Using this representation of the rotation, the rotation matrix can be written as: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{R}_{\Delta t} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos \theta_Z & \sin \theta_Z & 0\\ -\sin \theta_Z & \cos \theta_Z & 0\\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \cos \theta_Y & 0 & -\sin \theta_Y\\ 0 & 1 & 0\\ \sin \theta_Y & 0 & \cos \theta_Y \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & \cos \theta_X & \sin \theta_X \\ 0 & -\sin \theta_X & \cos \theta_X \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$ In this equation, the sign of the angles are chosen to reflect that a rotation of the camera is equivalent to the opposite rotation of the 3D point.

concepts.title: Small Motion Rotation Approximation
concepts.one_liner: For small time intervals, rotation matrices can be approximated using small-angle assumptions to simplify the relationship between 3D points and motion.
concepts.content: For a small $\Delta t$, the angles will be small, and we can approximate the trigonometric functions by $\cos \alpha \approx 1$ and $\sin \alpha \approx \alpha$. We can also approximate the product $\sin \alpha \sin \beta \approx 0$ as it results in a second-order term. Under these assumptions, the rotation matrix simplifies to: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{R}_{\Delta t} \approx \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \theta_Z & 0\\ -\theta_Z & 1& 0\\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -\theta_Y\\ 0 & 1 & 0\\ \theta_Y & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & 1 & \theta_X \\ 0 & -\theta_X & 1 \end{bmatrix} \approx \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \theta_Z & -\theta_Y\\ -\theta_Z & 1 & \theta_X \\ \theta_Y & -\theta_X & 1 \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$ The change in position of a point $\mathbf{P}$ is then: $$\mathbf{P}_{t+\Delta t} - \mathbf{P}_{t} = - \mathbf{T}_{\Delta t} + (\mathbf{R}_{\Delta t} - \mathbf{I}) \mathbf{P}_t = - \mathbf{T}_{\Delta t} - \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -\theta_Z & \theta_Y\\ \theta_Z & 0 & -\theta_X \\ -\theta_Y & \theta_X & 0 \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{P}_t$$ The last term corresponds to the cross product in matrix form, allowing the expression to be rewritten as: $$\mathbf{P}_{t+\Delta t} - \mathbf{P}_{t} = - \mathbf{T}_{\Delta t} - \boldsymbol{\theta} \times \mathbf{P}_t$$
concepts.motivation_md: Linearizing rotation for small displacements simplifies complex trigonometric equations into a linear form involving cross products, making it computationally efficient to estimate motion in real-time applications.
concepts.recap_md: - Small angles allow the approximations $\cos \alpha \approx 1$ and $\sin \alpha \approx \alpha$.

We can also approximate the product $\sin \alpha \sin \beta \approx 0$ as it results in a second-order term. Under these assumptions, the rotation matrix simplifies to: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{R}_{\Delta t} \approx \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \theta_Z & 0\\ -\theta_Z & 1& 0\\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -\theta_Y\\ 0 & 1 & 0\\ \theta_Y & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & 1 & \theta_X \\ 0 & -\theta_X & 1 \end{bmatrix} \approx \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \theta_Z & -\theta_Y\\ -\theta_Z & 1 & \theta_X \\ \theta_Y & -\theta_X & 1 \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$ The change in position of a point $\mathbf{P}$ is then: $$\mathbf{P}_{t+\Delta t} - \mathbf{P}_{t} = - \mathbf{T}_{\Delta t} + (\mathbf{R}_{\Delta t} - \mathbf{I}) \mathbf{P}_t = - \mathbf{T}_{\Delta t} - \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -\theta_Z & \theta_Y\\ \theta_Z & 0 & -\theta_X \\ -\theta_Y & \theta_X & 0 \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{P}_t$$ The last term corresponds to the cross product in matrix form, allowing the expression to be rewritten as: $$\mathbf{P}_{t+\Delta t} - \mathbf{P}_{t} = - \mathbf{T}_{\Delta t} - \boldsymbol{\theta} \times \mathbf{P}_t$$

concepts.title: General 2D Motion Field Equation
concepts.one_liner: The general 2D motion field equation relates image plane velocity to the camera's translational and rotational velocities.
concepts.content: Substituting the small motion approximation into the general camera motion equation, we obtain the motion of a 3D point: $$\dot{\mathbf{P}} = - \mathbf{V} - \mathbf{W} \times \mathbf{P}_t = -\begin{bmatrix} V_X\\ V_Y \\ V_Z \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} -W_Z Y + W_Y Z\\ W_Z X - W_X Z \\ -W_Y X + W_X Y \end{bmatrix}$$ where $\mathbf{W}=(W_X,W_Y,W_Z)$ is the angular velocity. Using the projection equations $x=f \, X/Z$ and $y=f \, Y/Z$, the 2D motion field is: $$\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x} \\ \dot{y} \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{Z} \begin{bmatrix} -f & 0 & x \\ 0 & -f & y \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} V_X\\ V_Y \\ V_Z \end{bmatrix} + \frac{1}{f} \begin{bmatrix} xy & -f^2-x^2) & f y \\ f^2+y^2 & -xy & -f x \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} W_X\\ W_Y \\ W_Z \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$ This expression relates the 2D motion field with camera velocity and rotation. The matrices are functions of intrinsic camera parameters (focal length $f$) and camera coordinates. Note that this expression is only valid for small displacements.
concepts.motivation_md: This equation is fundamental for computer vision as it provides a mathematical link between the observed flow of pixels and the physical movement of the camera in 3D space.
concepts.recap_md: - The motion field is the sum of a translational component and a rotational component.

slots.example: Substituting the small motion approximation into the general camera motion equation, we obtain the motion of a 3D point: $$\dot{\mathbf{P}} = - \mathbf{V} - \mathbf{W} \times \mathbf{P}_t = -\begin{bmatrix} V_X\\ V_Y \\ V_Z \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} -W_Z Y + W_Y Z\\ W_Z X - W_X Z \\ -W_Y X + W_X Y \end{bmatrix}$$ where $\mathbf{W}=(W_X,W_Y,W_Z)$ is the angular velocity. Using the projection equations $x=f \, X/Z$ and $y=f \, Y/Z$, the 2D motion field is: $$\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x} \\ \dot{y} \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{Z} \begin{bmatrix} -f & 0 & x \\ 0 & -f & y \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} V_X\\ V_Y \\ V_Z \end{bmatrix} + \frac{1}{f} \begin{bmatrix} xy & -f^2-x^2) & f y \\ f^2+y^2 & -xy & -f x \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} W_X\\ W_Y \\ W_Z \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$ This expression relates the 2D motion field with camera velocity and rotation. The matrices are functions of intrinsic camera parameters (focal length $f$) and camera coordinates. Note that this expression is only valid for small displacements.

concepts.title: Camera Rotation Motion Field
concepts.one_liner: When a camera only rotates, the resulting 2D motion field depends solely on rotational velocity and camera parameters, independent of scene depth.
concepts.content: In the case where there is only camera rotation ($V_X=V_Y=V_Z=0$), the motion field equation simplifies to: $$\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x} \\ \dot{y} \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{f} \begin{bmatrix} xy & -f^2-x^2) & f y \\ f^2+y^2 & -xy & -f x \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} W_X\\ W_Y \\ W_Z \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$ The 2D motion field does not depend on the 3D scene structure $Z$ and is only a function of the rotational velocity and the camera parameters. Therefore, under pure camera rotation, we cannot learn anything about the scene structure by observing the motion field. The only information that can be extracted from the 2D motion field is the motion of the camera itself.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding pure rotation is crucial because it reveals a fundamental limitation: rotation alone provides no information about the distance to objects in the scene, unlike translation.
concepts.recap_md: - Pure rotational motion fields are independent of the scene's depth $Z$.

concepts.title: Rotation Around Optical Axis
concepts.one_liner: Rotation around the camera's optical axis creates a motion field where vectors are orthogonal to the radial vector from the image origin.
concepts.content: Consider rotation along the camera optical axis, where $W_X=W_Y=0$. In this case, the motion field is: $$\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x} \\ \dot{y} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} y \\ -x \end{bmatrix} W_Z \end{aligned}$$ The 2D motion field at each location $(x,y)$ points in the orthogonal direction to the vector that connects that point with the origin (see figure: Motion field for a rotating camera around the optical axis, $W_X=W_Y=0$.). This motion field does not depend on the focal length $f$.
concepts.motivation_md: This case isolates the effect of 'roll' on the image, showing that it produces a simple circular flow pattern that is invariant to the camera's focal length.
concepts.recap_md: - Rotation around the $Z$-axis (optical axis) results in a circular motion field.

slots.key_passage: - Rotation around the $Z$-axis (optical axis) results in a circular motion field.
slots.example: Consider rotation along the camera optical axis, where $W_X=W_Y=0$. In this case, the motion field is: $$\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x} \\ \dot{y} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} y \\ -x \end{bmatrix} W_Z \end{aligned}$$ The 2D motion field at each location $(x,y)$ points in the orthogonal direction to the vector that connects that point with the origin (see figure: Motion field for a rotating camera around the optical axis, $W_X=W_Y=0$.). This motion field does not depend on the focal length $f$.

concepts.title: Rotation Around Y-Axis
concepts.one_liner: Rotation around the Y-axis produces a motion field heavily influenced by focal length, appearing as lateral translation for large focal lengths.
concepts.content: If $W_Z=0$ and $W_X=0$, rotation along the $Y$-axis ($W_Y$) produces the following motion field: $$\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x} \\ \dot{y} \end{bmatrix} = -\frac{1}{f} \begin{bmatrix} f^2+x^2 \\ xy \end{bmatrix} W_Y \end{aligned}$$ The focal length $f$ has a strong effect on the appearance of this motion field. For very large $f$, the 2D motion field can be approximated by $\dot{x} \approx f W_Y$ and $\dot{y} \approx 0$, which looks like lateral translation. For very small $f$, the field is similar to a homography and differs significantly from lateral camera motion. The flows shown in (see figure: Motion flows corresponding to a rotation around the Y-axis.) correspond to $f=1/3$, $f=1$, and $f=3$. Camera rotation around the $Y$-axis does not inform about scene structure, but it does inform about camera parameters. The magnitude of $W_Y$ only affects the scaling of the motion vectors, but it does not change their orientation.
concepts.motivation_md: Analyzing Y-axis rotation (yaw) helps distinguish between true camera translation and rotation, especially since they can look similar at high zoom levels.
concepts.recap_md: - Rotation around the $Y$-axis produces a motion field sensitive to focal length $f$.

concepts.title: Motion under Varying Focal Length
concepts.one_liner: Changing the focal length of a static camera creates a motion field that scales the image without providing depth information.
concepts.content: Consider a static camera observing a static scene where the focal length $f$ changes over time. This produces motion in the image plane; an increasing focal length results in a zoom effect. Starting from the perspective projection equation: $$\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \frac{f}{Z} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$ Computing the temporal derivative where only $f$ varies gives: $$\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x} \\ \dot{y} \end{bmatrix} = \frac{\dot{f}}{Z} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \end{bmatrix} = \frac{\dot{f}}{f} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$ This expression shows that changing the focal length results in a scaling of the projected image on the image plane. It does not create parallax. Because the sensor has a finite size, changing the focal length results in a zoom and a crop. Crucially, the motion field does not depend on the 3D scene structure $Z$, meaning images taken from the same viewpoint with different focal lengths do not provide depth information.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept explains why 'zooming' is fundamentally different from 'moving forward'—zooming is a purely 2D image transformation that lacks the depth cues (parallax) provided by physical camera movement.
concepts.recap_md: - Changing focal length (zooming) creates a radial motion field from the image center.

concepts.title: Perspective Projection Equations for Motion
concepts.one_liner: The temporal derivative of the perspective projection equation describes how image coordinates change when the focal length varies.
concepts.content: Starting from the perspective projection equation: $$\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \frac{f}{Z} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$ If we compute the temporal derivative where only the focal length $f$ varies over time, we obtain: $$\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x} \\ \dot{y} \end{bmatrix} = \frac{\dot{f}}{Z} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \end{bmatrix} = \frac{\dot{f}}{f} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: These equations provide the mathematical basis for understanding how optical zoom affects the position of points on the image sensor over time.
concepts.recap_md: - The motion field $(\dot{x}, \dot{y})$ is proportional to the current coordinates $(x, y)$ when only $f$ changes.

slots.motivation: These equations provide the mathematical basis for understanding how optical zoom affects the position of points on the image sensor over time.
slots.key_passage: - The motion field $(\dot{x}, \dot{y})$ is proportional to the current coordinates $(x, y)$ when only $f$ changes.
slots.example: Starting from the perspective projection equation: $$\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \frac{f}{Z} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$ If we compute the temporal derivative where only the focal length $f$ varies over time, we obtain: $$\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x} \\ \dot{y} \end{bmatrix} = \frac{\dot{f}}{Z} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \end{bmatrix} = \frac{\dot{f}}{f} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$

prereq.rationale: Time to contact is defined based on the ratio of depth to velocity during forward camera translation.
The focus of expansion is a characteristic point within the motion field generated by forward camera translation.
The small motion approximation simplifies the full Euler angle rotation matrix for small time intervals.
The general motion field equation incorporates the translational component derived earlier.
The rotational component of the general motion field is derived using the small motion approximation.
The conceptual understanding of the zoom effect is supported by the mathematical derivation of the perspective projection's temporal derivative.

overlay.rationale: The vanishing point of a moving point is the limit of the motion field as time goes to infinity.
Lateral camera motion is the specific case of the translation motion field where the forward velocity component Vz is zero.
Forward motion is the specific case of the translation motion field where lateral velocity components Vx and Vy are zero.
The focus of expansion is the specific vanishing point for the case of a camera moving forward along its optical axis.
The rotation-only motion field is a special case of the general equation where translational velocity V is zero.
Unlike translation, pure rotation produces a motion field that is independent of scene depth Z, meaning no structure can be recovered.
Rotation around the optical axis is a specific instance of the rotation motion field where Wx and Wy are zero.
Rotation around the Y-axis is a specific instance of the rotation motion field where Wx and Wz are zero.
